content.prompt: Check whether or not each point lies on the circle $x^2+y^2=100$.

answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=6^2+8^2\\x^2+y^2&=36+64\\x^2+y^2&=100\end{align*}$$
The point lies on the circle.

$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=10^2+10^2\\x^2+y^2&=100+100\\x^2+y^2&=200\end{align*}$$
Since $200\ne100$, the point does not lie on the circle.

$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=20^2+80^2\\x^2+y^2&=400+6400\\x^2+y^2&=6800\end{align*}$$
Since $6800\ne100$, the point does not lie on the circle.

$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=(-6)^2+8^2\\x^2+y^2&=36+64\\x^2+y^2&=100\end{align*}$$
The point lies on the circle.

$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=(5\sqrt{2})^2+(5\sqrt{2})^2\\x^2+y^2&=25\times2+25\times2\\x^2+y^2&=100\end{align*}$$
The point lies on the circle.

$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2&=10^2+0^2\\x^2+y^2&=100+0\\x^2+y^2&=100\end{align*}$$
The point lies on the circle.

content.prompt: Sketch the graphs, showing the $x$- and $y$-intercepts.

answer.worked:
Centre $(1,2)$ and radius $2$.

For the $x$-intercept, put $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}(x-1)^2+(0-2)^2&=4\\(x-1)^2&=0\\x&=1\end{align*}$$
For the $y$-intercepts, put $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}(0-1)^2+(y-2)^2&=4\\(y-2)^2&=3\\y-2&=\pm\sqrt3\\y&=2\pm\sqrt3\end{align*}$$
The circle touches the $x$-axis at $(1,0)$.

spec.description: Unfilled circle with labelled centre and all intercepts; tangent to the horizontal axis.

answer.worked:

Put $y=0$:
$$\begin{align*}(x-3)^2+(0-4)^2&=25\\(x-3)^2&=9\\x-3&=\pm3\\x&=0\text{ or }6\end{align*}$$
Put $x=0$:
$$\begin{align*}(0-3)^2+(y-4)^2&=25\\(y-4)^2&=16\\y-4&=\pm4\\y&=0\text{ or }8\end{align*}$$
Sketch the circle through $(0,0)$, $(6,0)$ and $(0,8)$.

content.prompt: Show that the point $(17,17)$ lies on the circle with centre $(5,12)$ and radius $13$. Find the equation of the circle.

answer.short:
The distance from $(5,12)$ to $(17,17)$ is $\sqrt{12^2+5^2}=13$, equal to the radius, so the point lies on the circle.

$(x-5)^2+(y-12)^2=169$.
answer.worked:
The distance from the centre to the point is
$$\begin{align*}d&=\sqrt{(17-5)^2+(17-12)^2}\\d&=\sqrt{144+25}\\d&=13.\end{align*}$$
This equals the radius, so $(17,17)$ lies on the circle.

Using the centre $(5,12)$ and radius $13$:
$$\begin{align*}(x-5)^2+(y-12)^2&=13^2\\(x-5)^2+(y-12)^2&=169.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Show that the line $y=2x$ does not meet the circle $(x-5)^2+y^2=4$.

answer.short:
The line does not meet the circle.

Substitution gives $5x^2-10x+21=0$, whose discriminant is $-320<0$, so there are no real intersection points.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=2x$ into the circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}(x-5)^2+(2x)^2&=4\\x^2-10x+25+4x^2&=4\\5x^2-10x+21&=0.
\end{align*}$$
For this quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=b^2-4ac\\\Delta&=(-10)^2-4(5)(21)\\\Delta&=100-420\\\Delta&=-320<0.
\end{align*}$$
There are no real solutions, so the line does not meet the circle.

content.prompt: Find the values of $a$ for which the graphs of $y=x+a$ and $x^2+y^2=9$ intersect at:

answer.short:
$a=3\sqrt{2}$ or $a=-3\sqrt{2}$.

One intersection requires a zero discriminant.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=x+a$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(x+a)^2&=9\\2x^2+2ax+a^2-9&=0\\\Delta&=(2a)^2-4(2)(a^2-9)\\\Delta&=72-4a^2\end{align*}$$
One intersection requires equal roots, so $\Delta=0$.
$$\begin{align*}72-4a^2&=0\\a^2&=18\\a&=\pm3\sqrt{2}\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$-3\sqrt{2}<a<3\sqrt{2}$.

Two intersections require a positive discriminant.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=x+a$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(x+a)^2&=9\\2x^2+2ax+a^2-9&=0\\\Delta&=(2a)^2-4(2)(a^2-9)\\\Delta&=72-4a^2\end{align*}$$
Two intersections require two distinct real roots, so $\Delta>0$.
$$\begin{align*}72-4a^2&>0\\a^2&<18\end{align*}$$
Therefore $-3\sqrt{2}<a<3\sqrt{2}$.

answer.short:
$a<-3\sqrt{2}$ or $a>3\sqrt{2}$.

No intersections require a negative discriminant.
answer.worked:
Substitute $y=x+a$ into the circle equation.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(x+a)^2&=9\\2x^2+2ax+a^2-9&=0\\\Delta&=(2a)^2-4(2)(a^2-9)\\\Delta&=72-4a^2\end{align*}$$
No intersections require no real roots, so $\Delta<0$.
$$\begin{align*}72-4a^2&<0\\a^2&>18\end{align*}$$
Therefore $a<-3\sqrt{2}$ or $a>3\sqrt{2}$.

answer.short:
Centre $\left(2,-\frac54\right)$; radius $\frac{\sqrt{65}}4$.

Divide by $2$, then complete the square in both variables.
answer.worked:
Divide by $2$.
$$\begin{align*}x^2+y^2-4x+\frac52y+\frac32&=0\\(x^2-4x)+\left(y^2+\frac52y\right)&=-\frac32\\(x^2-4x+4)+\left(y^2+\frac52y+\frac{25}{16}\right)&=-\frac32+4+\frac{25}{16}\\(x-2)^2+\left(y+\frac54\right)^2&=\frac{65}{16}\end{align*}$$
Centre $\left(2,-\frac54\right)$; radius $\sqrt{\frac{65}{16}}=\frac{\sqrt{65}}4$.

answer.short: Asymptotes: $x=-2$ and $y=0$. The $y$-intercept is $\left(0,\frac12\right)$; there are no $x$-intercepts.

Translate $y=\frac1x$ two units left. The vertical asymptote is $x=-2$ and the horizontal asymptote is $y=0$.

content.prompt: Find the points where each parabola meets the line.

answer.worked:
At an intersection, the two expressions for $y$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}2x^2-3x+4&=12-3x\\2x^2&=8\\x^2&=4\\x&=-2\text{ or }2\end{align*}$$
When $x=-2$, $y=12-3(-2)=18$.

When $x=2$, $y=12-3(2)=6$.

The points are $(-2,18)$ and $(2,6)$.

At an intersection, the two expressions for $y$ are equal.
$$\begin{align*}2-x-3x^2&=-7x+2\\3x^2-6x&=0\\3x(x-2)&=0\\x&=0\text{ or }2\end{align*}$$
When $x=0$, $y=-7(0)+2=2$.

When $x=2$, $y=-7(2)+2=-12$.

The points are $(0,2)$ and $(2,-12)$.

content.prompt: Find the points of intersection of:

answer.worked:
Substitute $x=3$ into the circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}3^2+y^2&=9\\y^2&=0\\y&=0\end{align*}$$
The point of intersection is $(3,0)$.

Substitute $y=0$ into the circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+0^2&=16\\x^2&=16\\x&=\pm4\end{align*}$$
The points of intersection are $(-4,0)$ and $(4,0)$.

Substitute $y=\sqrt{3}x$ into the circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(\sqrt{3}x)^2&=16\\x^2+3x^2&=16\\4x^2&=16\\x^2&=4\\x&=\pm2\end{align*}$$
When $x=-2$, $y=\sqrt{3}(-2)=-2\sqrt{3}$.

When $x=2$, $y=\sqrt{3}(2)=2\sqrt{3}$.

The points of intersection are $(-2,-2\sqrt{3})$ and $(2,2\sqrt{3})$.

content.prompt: Find the points of intersection of:

answer.worked:
From the line, $y=\dfrac{25-4x}{3}$. Substitute into the circle:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\left(\frac{25-4x}{3}\right)^2&=25\\9x^2+(25-4x)^2&=225\\9x^2+625-200x+16x^2&=225\\25x^2-200x+400&=0\\x^2-8x+16&=0\\(x-4)^2&=0\\x&=4.
\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac{25-4(4)}{3}\\y&=3.
\end{align*}$$
There is one point of intersection, $(4,3)$.

Substitute $y=3x-1$ into the circle:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+(3x-1)^2&=29\\x^2+9x^2-6x+1&=29\\10x^2-6x-28&=0\\5x^2-3x-14&=0\\(5x+7)(x-2)&=0\\x&=-\frac75\text{ or }2.
\end{align*}$$
When $x=-\dfrac75$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=3\left(-\frac75\right)-1\\y&=-\frac{26}5.
\end{align*}$$
When $x=2$:
$$\begin{align*}y&=3(2)-1\\y&=5.
\end{align*}$$
The points of intersection are $\left(-\dfrac75,-\dfrac{26}5\right)$ and $(2,5)$.

content.prompt: Find the points where the hyperbola meets the line.

answer.worked:
Equating the expressions for $y$, with $x\ne0$:
$$\begin{align*}x-1&=\frac{12}{x}\\x^2-x&=12\\x^2-x-12&=0\\(x-4)(x+3)&=0\\x&=4\text{ or }-3.\end{align*}$$
For $x=4$, $y=4-1=3$. For $x=-3$, $y=-3-1=-4$.
The intersection points are $(4,3)$ and $(-3,-4)$.

Equating the expressions for $y$, with $x\ne0$:
$$\begin{align*}2x-7&=-\frac{3}{x}\\2x^2-7x&=-3\\2x^2-7x+3&=0\\(2x-1)(x-3)&=0\\x&=\frac12\text{ or }3.\end{align*}$$
For $x=\frac12$, $y=2\left(\frac12\right)-7=-6$. For $x=3$, $y=2(3)-7=-1$.
The intersection points are $\left(\frac12,-6\right)$ and $(3,-1)$.

Substitute $x=3$ into the hyperbola equation:
$$\begin{align*}y&=\frac63\\y&=2.\end{align*}$$
The intersection point is $(3,2)$.

answer.short:
No points of intersection.

The resulting quadratic has a negative discriminant.
answer.worked:
Equating the expressions for $y$, with $x\ne0$:
$$\begin{align*}4-x&=\frac9x\\4x-x^2&=9\\x^2-4x+9&=0.\end{align*}$$
For this quadratic:
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-4)^2-4(1)(9)\\\Delta&=16-36\\\Delta&=-20<0.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: Triangle $ABC$ is equilateral with vertices $A(0,a)$, $B(m,0)$ and $C(-m,0)$.

spec.description: Equilateral triangle with horizontal base on the x-axis, upper vertex on the positive y-axis and its circumcircle extending below the x-axis. X is not marked. Source blue outlines and red vertex dots become ordinary black marks under house style; the origin O label is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: Representative coordinates use m=1 and a=sqrt(3); the circumcentre is (0,sqrt(3)/3) and radius is 2sqrt(3)/3. These construction coordinates are not printed numerical givens.
spec.answerVisibility: Supplied figure remains visible in every edition; no perpendicular bisectors or X are supplied.

answer.worked:
Since the triangle is equilateral, $AB=BC=2m$. By Pythagoras,
$$\begin{align*}a^2+m^2&=(2m)^2\\a^2&=3m^2\\a&=\sqrt{3}m.\end{align*}$$
The positive root is used because $A$ is above the $x$-axis and $B$ is on its positive side.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find, in terms of $a$, the equation of the perpendicular bisector of:

answer.worked:
The midpoint of $AC$ is $(-m/2,a/2)$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Gradient of }AC&=\frac{a-0}{0-(-m)}\\\text{Gradient of }AC&=\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
The perpendicular gradient is $-1/\sqrt{3}$. Using the midpoint,
$$\begin{align*}y-\frac a2&=-\frac1{\sqrt{3}}\left(x+\frac m2\right)\\y&=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a2-\frac a6\\y&=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a3.\end{align*}$$

The midpoint of $AB$ is $(m/2,a/2)$.
$$\begin{align*}\text{Gradient of }AB&=\frac{0-a}{m-0}\\\text{Gradient of }AB&=-\sqrt{3}.\end{align*}$$
The perpendicular gradient is $1/\sqrt{3}$. Using the midpoint,
$$\begin{align*}y-\frac a2&=\frac1{\sqrt{3}}\left(x-\frac m2\right)\\y&=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a2-\frac a6\\y&=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a3.\end{align*}$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Show that the two perpendicular bisectors meet at $X\left(0,\dfrac a3\right)$.

answer.worked:
At the intersection, the two expressions for $y$ are equal:
$$\begin{align*}-\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a3&=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}+\frac a3\\\frac{2x}{\sqrt{3}}&=0\\x&=0.\end{align*}$$
Substitution into either equation gives $y=a/3$, so the intersection is $X(0,a/3)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find the distance $AX$ in terms of $a$.

answer.worked:
Both points lie on the $y$-axis, with $A$ above $X$:
$$\begin{align*}AX&=a-\frac a3\\AX&=\frac{2a}{3}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the equation of the circle with centre $X\left(0,\dfrac a3\right)$ and radius $AX$.

answer.worked:
Use $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$ with centre $(0,a/3)$ and radius $2a/3$:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\left(y-\frac a3\right)^2&=\left(\frac{2a}{3}\right)^2\\x^2+\left(y-\frac a3\right)^2&=\frac{4a^2}{9}.\end{align*}$$

children.label: i
children.prompt: Use the fact that $XY$ is perpendicular to $ZY$ to show that $x^2+y^2=a^2$.

answer.worked:
The gradients are $m_{XY}=\dfrac{y}{x-a}$ and $m_{ZY}=\dfrac{y}{x+a}$. Since $XY\perp ZY$,

$$\begin{align*}\frac{y}{x-a}\cdot\frac{y}{x+a}&=-1\\\frac{y^2}{x^2-a^2}&=-1\\y^2&=a^2-x^2\\x^2+y^2&=a^2.\end{align*}$$

answer.short:
$OX=OY=OZ=|a|$.

Use the distance from the origin and the result in part i.
answer.worked:
Using part i and the distance formula,

$$\begin{align*}OY&=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\\OY&=\sqrt{a^2}\\OY&=|a|.\end{align*}$$

Also $OX=OZ=|a|$, so $OX=OY=OZ$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: $P(x,y)$ is a point on the circle $x^2+y^2=a^2$. Show that $PA$ is perpendicular to $PB$.

spec.description: Dashed circle centred at the origin, horizontal diameter AB and chords PA and PB, with P on the upper-left arc. Bare origin O is omitted under the graph convention.
spec.mathematics: A=(-a,0), B=(a,0), and P=(x,y) lies on x^2+y^2=a^2. P is distinct from the diameter endpoints.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied locus and chords are visible; no right-angle conclusion is drawn.

answer.short:
$PA\perp PB$.

Their gradients have product $-1$, using $x^2+y^2=a^2$.
answer.worked:
For $P$ distinct from $A$ and $B$, the gradients are $m_{PA}=\dfrac{y}{x+a}$ and $m_{PB}=\dfrac{y}{x-a}$. Since $x^2+y^2=a^2$, we have $y^2=a^2-x^2$.

$$\begin{align*}m_{PA}m_{PB}&=\frac{y}{x+a}\cdot\frac{y}{x-a}\\m_{PA}m_{PB}&=\frac{y^2}{x^2-a^2}\\m_{PA}m_{PB}&=\frac{a^2-x^2}{x^2-a^2}\\m_{PA}m_{PB}&=-1.\end{align*}$$

Therefore $PA\perp PB$.

content.prompt: $ABCO$ is a square of side length $a$. Show that the equation of the circle passing through all four vertices is $x^2+y^2-ax-ay=0$.

spec.description: Unshaded square in the first quadrant, with its left and bottom sides on the coordinate axes. Preserve the labelled vertex O(0,0); no additional origin label is drawn. Decorative source blue edges and red vertex markers become black.

answer.short:
The centre is $\left(\frac a2,\frac a2\right)$ and the radius is $\frac{a\sqrt2}{2}$.

Substitute these into the standard circle equation and expand to obtain $x^2+y^2-ax-ay=0$.
answer.worked:
The diagonals of the square bisect each other, so their intersection is $\left(\frac a2,\frac a2\right)$. This point is equidistant from all four vertices and is therefore the circle's centre.

Using the distance to $O(0,0)$,
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=\left(\frac a2\right)^2+\left(\frac a2\right)^2\\r^2&=\frac{a^2}{2},\\r&=\frac{a\sqrt2}{2}.\end{align*}$$
The standard circle equation gives
$$\begin{align*}\left(x-\frac a2\right)^2+\left(y-\frac a2\right)^2&=\frac{a^2}{2}\\x^2-ax+\frac{a^2}{4}+y^2-ay+\frac{a^2}{4}&=\frac{a^2}{2}\\x^2+y^2-ax-ay&=0.\end{align*}$$

content.prompt: The points $O(0,0)$, $A(a,0)$ and $B(0,b)$ lie on a circle.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of:

answer.worked:
The midpoint of $OA$ is $\left(\dfrac{0+a}{2},\dfrac{0+0}{2}\right)=\left(\dfrac a2,0\right)$. Since $OA$ is horizontal, its perpendicular bisector is vertical:

$$x=\frac a2.$$

The midpoint of $OB$ is $\left(\dfrac{0+0}{2},\dfrac{0+b}{2}\right)=\left(0,\dfrac b2\right)$. Since $OB$ is vertical, its perpendicular bisector is horizontal:

$$y=\frac b2.$$

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the coordinates of the point of intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of $OA$ and $OB$.

answer.worked: At the intersection, $x=\dfrac a2$ and $y=\dfrac b2$. Hence the point is $\left(\dfrac a2,\dfrac b2\right)$.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Show that the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ also passes through this point.

answer.short: The midpoint of $AB$ is $\left(\dfrac a2,\dfrac b2\right)$, so its perpendicular bisector passes through this point.
answer.worked:
Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$.

$$M=\left(\frac{a+0}{2},\frac{0+b}{2}\right)=\left(\frac a2,\frac b2\right).$$

This is the point found in part b. The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ passes through its midpoint, so it passes through this point.

Using gradients also gives

$$\begin{align*}m_{AB}&=\frac{b-0}{0-a}\\m_{AB}&=-\frac ba.\end{align*}$$

Its perpendicular bisector has gradient $\dfrac ab$ and equation

$$y-\frac b2=\frac ab\left(x-\frac a2\right).$$

Substituting $\left(\dfrac a2,\dfrac b2\right)$ gives $0=0$.

children.label: d
children.prompt: Find the equation of the circle passing through $O$, $A$ and $B$.

answer.short:
$\left(x-\dfrac a2\right)^2+\left(y-\dfrac b2\right)^2=\dfrac{a^2+b^2}{4}$

The centre is the intersection of the perpendicular bisectors; find the radius using its distance from $O$.
answer.worked:
The centre is $C\left(\dfrac a2,\dfrac b2\right)$, where the perpendicular bisectors meet. Since $O$ lies on the circle,

$$\begin{align*}r^2&=\left(\frac a2-0\right)^2+\left(\frac b2-0\right)^2\\r^2&=\frac{a^2+b^2}{4}.\end{align*}$$

Using the standard circle equation,

$$\left(x-\frac a2\right)^2+\left(y-\frac b2\right)^2=\frac{a^2+b^2}{4}.$$

content.prompt: Find the equation of the circle that passes through the points $(a,b)$, $(a,-b)$ and $(a+b,a-b)$.

answer.short:
$$\left(x-\frac{a^2+b^2}{2b}\right)^2+y^2=\frac{(a-b)^4+4b^4}{4b^2},\qquad b\ne0.$$

Substitute the three points into the standard circle equation and compare the resulting equations.
answer.worked:
Let the circle have equation $(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2=r^2$. Substituting the first two points gives
$$\begin{align*}(a-h)^2+(b-k)^2&=r^2\\(a-h)^2+(-b-k)^2&=r^2.\end{align*}$$
Subtracting these equations gives $-4bk=0$, so $k=0$ when $b\ne0$. Substituting the first and third points now gives
$$\begin{align*}(a-h)^2+b^2&=r^2\\(a+b-h)^2+(a-b)^2&=r^2.\end{align*}$$
Subtracting the first equation from the second,
$$\begin{align*}2b(a-h)+b^2+(a-b)^2-b^2&=0\\a^2+b^2-2bh&=0\\h&=\frac{a^2+b^2}{2b}.\end{align*}$$
Hence
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=\left(a-\frac{a^2+b^2}{2b}\right)^2+b^2\\r^2&=\frac{(a-b)^4}{4b^2}+b^2\\r^2&=\frac{(a-b)^4+4b^4}{4b^2}.\end{align*}$$
Therefore
$$\boxed{\left(x-\frac{a^2+b^2}{2b}\right)^2+y^2=\frac{(a-b)^4+4b^4}{4b^2}}\qquad(b\ne0).$$

answer.short:
$\displaystyle \left(x-\frac52\right)^2+y^2=\frac54$.

The perpendicular radius locates the centre at $\left(\frac52,0\right)$.
answer.worked:
Let the centre be $C(h,0)$, as shown in the diagram. The radius $CA$ is perpendicular to the line of gradient $\frac12$, so its gradient is $-2$. Through $A(2,1)$, the radius lies on
$$\begin{align*}y-1&=-2(x-2)\\y&=-2x+5.\end{align*}$$
At the centre, $y=0$, so $h=\frac52$. Using $A(2,1)$,
$$\begin{align*}r^2&=\left(2-\frac52\right)^2+(1-0)^2\\r^2&=\frac14+1\\r^2&=\frac54.\end{align*}$$
Hence the circle is $\displaystyle \left(x-\frac52\right)^2+y^2=\frac54$.

content.prompt: Show that the circles $x^2+y^2-2x-3y=0$ and $x^2+y^2+x-y=6$ intersect on the $x$-axis and $y$-axis.

answer.short:
The intersections are $(2,0)$ on the $x$-axis and $(0,3)$ on the $y$-axis.

Subtract the circle equations to obtain $3x+2y=6$, then substitute to find the two points.
answer.worked:
Subtracting the first circle equation from the second gives
$$\begin{align*}3x+2y&=6\\y&=3-\frac32x.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the first circle equation:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\left(3-\frac32x\right)^2-2x-3\left(3-\frac32x\right)&=0\\\frac{13}{4}x^2-\frac{13}{2}x&=0\\13x(x-2)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=0$ or $x=2$. When $x=0$, $y=3$; when $x=2$, $y=0$.

Both points satisfy the original equations: at $(0,3)$ their left-hand sides are $9-9=0$ and $9-3=6$; at $(2,0)$ they are $4-4=0$ and $4+2=6$.

Hence the circles intersect at $(2,0)$ on the $x$-axis and $(0,3)$ on the $y$-axis.

content.prompt: Find the points of intersection of the circles $x^2+y^2+x-3y=0$ and $2x^2+2y^2-x-2y-15=0$.

answer.short:
$\left(-\frac95,\frac{12}5\right)$ and $(-1,3)$.

Eliminate the quadratic terms, then substitute the resulting linear equation into either circle.
answer.worked:
Subtract twice the first equation from the second:
$$\begin{align*}-3x+4y-15&=0\\4y&=3x+15\\y&=\frac{3x+15}{4}.\end{align*}$$
Substitute into the first circle:
$$\begin{align*}x^2+\left(\frac{3x+15}{4}\right)^2+x-3\left(\frac{3x+15}{4}\right)&=0\\16x^2+(3x+15)^2+16x-12(3x+15)&=0\\25x^2+70x+45&=0\\5x^2+14x+9&=0\\(5x+9)(x+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $x=-\frac95$ or $x=-1$.

When $x=-\frac95$,
$$y=\frac{3(-9/5)+15}{4}=\frac{12}{5}.$$
When $x=-1$,
$$y=\frac{3(-1)+15}{4}=3.$$
The intersection points are $\left(-\frac95,\frac{12}5\right)$ and $(-1,3)$.

inlines.text: The general equation of a circle is
. Find the equation of the circle passing through the points

answer.short:
$x^2+y^2-x-5y+4=0$.

Substitute the three points into the general form and solve for its coefficients.
answer.worked:
Substituting the three points gives
$$\begin{align*}
-2g+6f+c&=-10 &&\text{from }(-1,3),\qquad\text{(1)}\\
4g+4f+c&=-8 &&\text{from }(2,2),\qquad\text{(2)}\\
2g+8f+c&=-17 &&\text{from }(1,4).\qquad\text{(3)}
\end{align*}$$
Subtracting (1) from (2), and (2) from (3), gives
$$\begin{align*}
6g-2f&=2,\\
-2g+4f&=-9.
\end{align*}$$
Twice the first equation plus the second gives
$$\begin{align*}
10g&=-5,\\
g&=-\frac12.
\end{align*}$$
Then
$$\begin{align*}
-3-2f&=2,\\
f&=-\frac52,\\
1-15+c&=-10,\\
c&=4.
\end{align*}$$
Hence the circle is $x^2+y^2-x-5y+4=0$.

content.prompt: Show that $y=ax+b$, where $a>0$, always meets $y=\dfrac{1}{x}$.

answer.short:
$\Delta=b^2+4a>0$ since $a>0$, so there are always two distinct points of intersection.

Eliminating $y$ gives $ax^2+bx-1=0$; neither root is zero.
answer.worked:
At an intersection, eliminate $y$:
$$\begin{align*}ax+b&=\frac{1}{x}\\ax^2+bx&=1\\ax^2+bx-1&=0.\end{align*}$$
For this quadratic,
$$\begin{align*}\Delta&=b^2-4a(-1)\\\Delta&=b^2+4a\\\Delta&>0,\end{align*}$$
since $b^2\geq0$ and $a>0$. Hence there are two distinct real roots. Neither root is zero, because substituting $x=0$ into $ax^2+bx-1$ gives $-1$. Each root therefore gives a valid point on both graphs, so the line always meets the hyperbola at two distinct points.

entries.description:
Circles with centre the origin
Consider a circle in the coordinate plane with centre the origin and radius r. Throughout this chapter, we will always assume that r > 0.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone teaching; retain as taught-method evidence, not an authored practice question.

entries.description: Circle centred at O on Cartesian axes labelled x and y. A first-quadrant point P(x, y) lies on the circle. Radius OP is labelled r. A perpendicular from P to the positive x-axis forms a right triangle with horizontal side x, vertical side y and a right-angle marker at the foot. The circle is labelled x² + y² = r².
entries.presentation: Blue circle and radius; grey axes and perpendicular scaffold; red point P. Diagram sits between the introductory paragraph and derivation.
entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram belonging to excluded standalone teaching; retain as reference evidence.

entries.description:
If P(x, y) is a point on the circle, then its distance from the origin is r. By Pythagoras’ theorem, this gives x² + y² = r².
Conversely, if a point P(x, y) satisfies the equation x² + y² = r², then its distance from O(0, 0) is √(x² + y²) = r, so it lies on the circle with centre the origin and radius r.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone derivation and converse; retain as taught-method evidence.

entries.description:
The circle has centre the origin and radius 5.
To verify that a point lies on the circle, we substitute the coordinates into x² + y² = 25.
The point (3, 4) lies on the circle, since 3² + 4² = 25.
The point (−3, 4) lies on the circle, since (−3)² + 4² = 25.
The point (−3, −4) lies on the circle, since (−3)² + (−4)² = 25.
The point (4, −3) lies on the circle, since (4)² + (−3)² = 25.

entries.sourceLabel: Circles with centre not the origin
entries.description:
Now take a circle in the coordinate plane with centre at the point C(h, k) and radius r.
If P(x, y) is a point on the circle, then by the distance formula:
(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and derivation; retained as taught-method evidence.

entries.description: Horizontal x and vertical y axes with positive arrowheads and origin O. A blue circle has its centre C(h, k) above and to the right of O. A blue radius labelled r joins the red centre point to a red point P(x, y) on the upper-right circumference. The circle crosses both axes.
entries.presentation: Centred beneath the distance-formula equation. Symbolic schematic with no numerical ticks or specified dimensions.
entries.exclusionReason: Meaningful mathematical diagram supporting excluded standalone teaching.

entries.description:
Conversely, if a point P(x, y) satisfies the equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², then its distance from (h, k) is r, so it lies on a circle with centre C(h, k) and radius r.
We call (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² the standard form for the equation of a circle.
entries.presentation: The phrase “standard form for the equation of a circle” is bold pink.
entries.exclusionReason: Standalone explanation and definition; retained as taught-method evidence.

entries.description:
• The circle with centre O(0, 0) and radius r has equation:
x² + y² = r²

entries.description:
Finding the centre and radius of a circle by completing the square
In Example 3a, we sketched the graph of (x − 3)² + (y + 2)² = 4.
Expanding the brackets, we obtain:
x² − 6x + 9 + y² + 4y + 4 = 4
which simplifies to:
x² + y² − 6x + 4y + 9 = 0
This is still the equation of the circle with centre (3, −2) and radius 2, but in this form it is not clear what the centre and radius are.
Completing the square enables us to reverse the process and to express the equation in standard form. We can then read off the centre and radius.

Can you see how these values are reflected in the graph close to the y-axis?
And as x gets larger and larger in the positive and negative directions (moves further away from zero), y gets smaller and smaller. For example, when x = 100, y = 0.01 and when x = 10 000, y = 0.0001. Similarly, when x = −100, y = −0.01 and when x = −10 000, y = −0.0001.

entries.description:
Features of y = 1/x
• There are no x-intercepts and no y-intercepts.
• When x is a large positive number, y is a small positive number.
• When x is a small positive number, y is a large positive number.
• Similar results hold for large and small negative values of x.
• The x-axis and the y-axis are called asymptotes to the graph. The graph gets very close to each of these lines, but never meets them.
• The lines y = x and y = −x are axes of symmetry for the graph of y = 1/x.

In this section we will look at the intersections of:
• lines and parabolas
• lines and circles
• lines and rectangular hyperbolas.
In Chapter 4, we looked at the intersections of lines.
Two distinct lines meet at zero points or 1 point. In the situations listed above, there are always 0, 1 or 2 points of intersection. We find these points of intersection by solving simultaneous equations.
That is, we shall be using algebra to solve problems in geometry.

entries.description:
To find the points of intersection, solve the equations simultaneously.
y = 4 − x²    (1)
y = 4 − x     (2)
At the points of intersection, the y-values are the same, so:
4 − x² = 4 − x
x² − x = 0
x(x − 1) = 0
x = 0 or x = 1
When x = 0, y = 4.
When x = 1, y = 3.
So the two points of intersection are (0, 4) and (1, 3).

entries.description: We have x² + y² = 5 (1); y = x + 1 (2). Substituting the right-hand side of (2) into (1): x² + (x + 1)² = 5; x² + x² + 2x + 1 = 5; 2x² + 2x − 4 = 0; x² + x − 2 = 0; (x + 2)(x − 1) = 0; x = −2 or x = 1. entries.description:
A straight line divides the plane into three non-overlapping regions:
• the points that lie on the line
• the points that lie on one side of the line
• the points that lie on the other side of the line.
Regions consisting of all the points on one side of a line are called half-planes.
The region may or may not include the points on the line. The line is often called the boundary line of the half-plane.

entries.description:
The region of the plane defined by the inequality y > x consists of all the points (x, y) whose y-coordinate is greater than the x-coordinate. The points (1, 2), (1, 3) and (1, 4) are all in this region, whereas (1, 0) and (1, −1) are not in the region.
The region y > x contains all the points above the line y = x. This is because if you choose any point on the line y = x (for example, (1, 1)), then all the points (x, y) above the point (1, 1) have y > x, and those below have y < x.
The region y > x is shown above. The line y = x is dashed to show that it is not included in the region y > x.

entries.description:
We first sketch the boundary line y = 2x + 1.
The boundary line has been drawn as a solid line since it is included in the required region.
Method 1 – Using the inequality with y the subject
If you choose any point on the line y = 2x + 1, for example, (0, 1), then all the points above (0, 1) have y ≥ 2x + 1 and those below have y < 2x + 1. Hence, we shade the region above the line y = 2x + 1.
Method 2 – Using a test point not on the boundary line
Test the point (0, 0). Since 0 ≤ 2 × 0 + 1, the point (0, 0) does not belong to the region. Hence, the required region is above the line.
